title: Reserve study or SIRS? Two reports, two sets of rules, one condo budget
seoTitle: Florida Condo Reserve Study vs. SIRS: The Difference
description: A SIRS is one kind of reserve study, with stricter rules. Here is what Florida law says about each, which reserves owners can vote to waive, and what to ask.
dek: Board notices use "reserve study" and "SIRS" as if they were the same thing. They overlap, but the law treats them differently, especially when owners want to vote reserves down. Here is the plain-words difference.
facebook: Your board says "reserve study." The state says "SIRS." Same thing? Not quite, and the difference decides which reserves owners can still vote to waive and which ones they can't touch.

body.text: Open a Florida condo budget packet this fall and you may see two phrases: "reserve study" and "SIRS." Some notices use them as if they mean the same thing. They are related, but Florida law handles them differently. The difference matters most at one moment: when owners are asked to vote on cutting or skipping reserves.
This is a plain-words guide to what the law says, not legal advice. For questions about your own building, ask your board, your association attorney, or the professional who prepared your study.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Reserves: money the association saves every year for big future repairs and replacements, like a new roof. Reserve study: the everyday name for a report that lists the building's big parts, how long each should last, what each will cost to replace, and how much to save each year. SIRS: the structural integrity reserve study, a specific reserve study that Florida law requires for condo buildings three or more habitable stories tall. Remaining useful life: how many more years an item is expected to last.
Every condo budget must have reserves

Start with the rule that covers almost every Florida condo, tall or short. Section 718.112(2)(f) of the Florida Statutes says the yearly budget must include reserve accounts for capital expenditures and deferred maintenance. Deferred maintenance means repair work that has been put off and will have to be paid for later.

The law names the minimum: roof replacement, building painting and pavement resurfacing, plus any other item whose deferred maintenance expense or replacement cost is more than $25,000, or a higher inflation-adjusted amount if one applies. The amount to save for each item is figured from its estimated remaining useful life and its estimated replacement cost or deferred maintenance expense.

In that section, the statute never uses the words "reserve study" on their own. It requires the reserve accounts and says how they are computed. The report or schedule your board uses to get those numbers is what most people call a reserve study.
A SIRS is a reserve study with stricter rules

Section 718.112(2)(g) adds a second, tougher layer for taller buildings. Each residential condo building three habitable stories or higher, as measured by the Florida Building Code, must have a structural integrity reserve study at least every 10 years. DBPR, the state agency that oversees condos, describes it as a study of the reserve funds needed for future major repairs and replacement.
A SIRS differs from a general reserve study in four ways:

items: Who prepares it. The law says a SIRS must be done by a Florida-licensed engineer or architect, or by a reserve specialist or professional reserve analyst certified by the Community Associations Institute or the Association of Professional Reserve Analysts.

What it covers. At minimum: the roof; the structure, including load-bearing walls and primary structural members; fireproofing and fire protection; plumbing; electrical; waterproofing and exterior painting; windows and exterior doors; and other items over the $25,000 threshold whose failure would hurt those parts.
How it is done. It is based on a visual inspection of those parts. It must give each item's remaining useful life and cost, and a funding plan with a recommended yearly reserve amount.
Reporting. Within 45 days of getting the study, the association must give each owner a copy, or a notice that a copy is available on request, and tell the state it has done so.

body.text: The deadline also differs. Most associations owed their first SIRS by December 31, 2025. Some that also had a milestone inspection due could combine the two, but the statute says no SIRS may be completed after December 31, 2026.
The big difference: what owners can vote away

Here is where the two really split. In an association controlled by the owners, rather than the developer, owners can vote to waive or reduce reserves. That takes "a majority of the total voting interests," which means more than half of all the votes in the whole association, not just more than half of the people who show up.

But for budgets adopted on or after December 31, 2024, that vote cannot touch reserves for SIRS items. DBPR's FAQ says it plainly: associations may not waive reserves, or use the reserves for other purposes, for the required SIRS items. The narrow exception is a multicondominium association with an alternative funding method the state has approved.

So in a building that needs a SIRS, owners may still be able to vote down reserves for things outside the SIRS list, such as pavement resurfacing. They cannot vote down reserves for the roof, structure, waterproofing and the other SIRS items. In a two-story condo, no SIRS is required, and all of the regular reserves can still be waived or reduced by that majority vote.

Two more points from the statute. SIRS items may be pooled, meaning saved in one shared account, only with other SIRS items. And for SIRS items, the budget's reserves must follow the findings and recommendations of the most recent SIRS. DBPR also notes that the law does not require reserves to be fully funded the day a study is finished, unless there is an immediate safety problem.

items: Find out how tall your building is under the law. Three or more habitable stories means a SIRS is required.
Look at the reserve page of your proposed budget. Ask which lines come from the SIRS and which come from the regular reserve schedule.
If you get a ballot to waive or reduce reserves, read which reserves it covers. A waiver should not include SIRS items, except in the narrow multicondominium case.
Ask who prepared the numbers and when. For a SIRS, the preparer must be one of the professionals the law lists.

body.text: If you are on the board:

items: Keep the SIRS items and the other reserve items clearly separated in the budget, so owners can see which ones a vote can and cannot change.
Check that your SIRS was finished, sent or offered to owners within 45 days, and reported to DBPR.
Before putting a reserve waiver to a vote, have your association attorney review the ballot and the proxy wording. The statute requires a specific warning on those proxies.
Send questions about your figures to the engineer, architect or reserve professional who prepared the study.

faq.q: What is the difference between a reserve study and a SIRS in Florida?
faq.a: A reserve study is the general name for a report on what a condo's big parts will cost to replace and how much to save. A SIRS is a specific reserve study required by section 718.112(2)(g) for buildings three habitable stories or taller, done by a licensed engineer or architect or a certified reserve professional, covering set items like the roof, structure and waterproofing.

faq.q: Does a two-story condo need a SIRS?
faq.a: No. Florida law requires a SIRS only for residential condo buildings three habitable stories or higher. A shorter building still must budget reserves for the roof, painting, paving and items over $25,000 under section 718.112(2)(f).

faq.q: Can condo owners vote to waive reserves in Florida?
faq.a: In an owner-controlled association, a majority of the total voting interests can waive or reduce reserves. For budgets adopted on or after December 31, 2024, that vote cannot apply to reserves for SIRS items, except for a multicondominium with a state-approved alternative funding method.

faq.q: Who can do a structural integrity reserve study?
faq.a: The law lists a Florida-licensed engineer or architect, or a reserve specialist or professional reserve analyst certified by the Community Associations Institute or the Association of Professional Reserve Analysts.

faq.q: Do condo reserves have to be fully funded right after the study?
faq.a: Not necessarily. DBPR's FAQ says the law does not require reserves to be fully funded at the completion of the reserve study, unless there is an immediate safety issue.
